extracted.intended_audience: general readers and comics enthusiasts (creators, publishers, collectors, librarians)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of comic-book formats, production practices, content standards, and collector/market valuation used to produce or assess comic books and related formats (graphic novels, webtoons, manga).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and visual presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comic books heavily rely on their organization and visual presentation. Authors focus on the frame of the page, size, orientation, and panel position in order to convey the book's content."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that page framing, panel layout and positioning are central to storytelling; production should consider page/frame composition, panel sequencing, and how visual elements guide reader flow. Components to manage include panels, speech bubbles, text lines, and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panels as sequential scenes / sequential art
rubrics_metrics.description: "A comic book ... is a publication that consists of comics art in the form of sequential panels that represent individual scenes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative clarity depends on clear sequencing of panels to represent time, action and scene changes; panels are often accompanied by descriptive prose and dialogue in word balloons. Panel transitions and pacing are essential production/evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech balloons and tail design
rubrics_metrics.description: "Speech balloons are convex containers that hold dialogue or other information. They are generally connected to a character via a tail element, which has an origin, path, tip, and directional point."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balloon shape, placement, and tail (origin/path/tip/direction) must clearly indicate speaker and reading order; design choices affect legibility and narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover format elements and cover copy
rubrics_metrics.description: "A common comic-book cover format displays the issue number, date, price and publisher along with an illustration and cover copy which may include a story's title."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover design serves identification and marketing functions; inclusion and placement of issue metadata (number, date, price, publisher) plus eye-catching illustration/cover copy are production expectations and evaluation points for marketability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation steps and production considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Creating a comic book involves several steps, including writing, drawing, and coloring, and must take into account directions, axes, data, and metrics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production is multi-stage (script, pencils, inks, lettering, coloring, lettering, final layout) and should account for visual directionality (reader flow/axes), technical metrics (page size, bleed, gutters), and data needed for printing/distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and format classification (comic book vs graphic novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the United States, the term 'comic book' is generally used for comics periodicals and trade paperbacks while 'graphic novel' is the term used for standalone books."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate labeling affects marketing, distribution channels, and audience expectations; historically 'graphic novel' often implies standalone, longer-form or book-style publication, while 'comic book' implies periodical issues or trade collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard size, format and page-count expectations by market
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and market formats are cited (e.g., Funnies on Parade established the size, duration, and format of the modern comic book; Dell Publishing's 36-page Famous Funnies; Italian mainstream monthly black-and-white digest format of ~100–132 pages; collections >200 pages; A4 annuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and evaluators should follow market-specific format norms (page counts, trim sizes, black-and-white vs color, periodicity) since expectations differ by country/segment and affect production costs, distribution, and reader acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content standards and censorship (Comics Code Authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The CMAA instilled the Comics Code Authority in 1954 and drafted the self-censorship Comics Code that year, which required all comic books to go through a process of approval."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, content had to meet the Code's restrictions to be approved for mainstream publication; creators/publishers should be aware of formal or informal content standards and their impact on distribution. (Note: the Code was made formally defunct in November 2011, but the example illustrates regulatory/self-regulatory influence on acceptable content.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground comix content expectations and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Underground comix ... most of such comics reflected the youth counterculture... Many had an uninhibited, often irreverent style; their frank depictions of nudity, sex, profanity, and politics had no parallel outside their precursors... Underground comics were almost never sold at newsstands, but rather in such youth-oriented outlets as head shops and record stores, as well as by mail order."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative/underground creators intentionally diverged from mainstream content standards; evaluation/production should account for explicitness, political or countercultural voice, and nontraditional distribution channels and ownership/rights considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Webtoon format and production considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Webtoons have become popular in South Korea as a new way to read comics. Thanks in part to different censorship rules, color and unique visual effects, and optimization for easier reading on smartphones and computers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital-first webtoon production prioritizes vertical scrolling layouts, full-color art, mobile optimization, and often animated/interactive visual effects; creators and evaluators should judge suitability for screen reading and platform-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collector valuation criteria (rarity, quality, first appearances)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most valuable American comics have combined rarity and quality with the first appearances of popular and enduring characters. The first issue of a long-running comic book series is commonly the rarest and most desirable to collectors. The first appearance of a specific character, however, might be in a pre-existing title..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collectors and appraisers evaluate scarcity (limited press runs, recalls, misprints), historical importance (first appearances), physical condition, and provenance. These factors drive market valuations and collecting priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading and conservation practices (CGC slabbing and numeric grades)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In 2000, a company named Comics Guaranty (CGC) began to 'slab' comics, encasing them in thick plastic and giving them a numeric grade."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional grading and encapsulation provide standardized numerical condition ratings that heavily influence market prices; preservation techniques and third-party certification are central to modern valuation and resale markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital distribution and publisher practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of digital distribution practices: "Marvel Digital Comics Unlimited, a subscription service allowing readers to read many comics... The service also includes periodic release new comics not available elsewhere. With the release of Avenging Spider-Man #1, Marvel also became the first publisher to provide free digital copies as part of the print copy... With the growing popularity of smartphones and tablets, many major publishers have begun releasing titles in digital form. The most popular platform is comiXology."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production and evaluation for digital releases must consider platform formats (file types, DRM), bundling strategies (print+digital offers), subscription access, discoverability, and how digital presentation affects reading experience (resolution, panel zooming, guided view).
